accuracy.evidence: Part names and jobs checked against the Year 1 Plants programme of study and NGSS 1-LS1-1: roots anchor and absorb water, the stem supports and carries water, leaves use light to make food, flowers make seeds; the trunk is a woody stem and branches are side stems. Food examples were chosen to be botanically clean (carrot and radish are roots, lettuce and spinach leaves, broccoli flower buds, asparagus a young stem) and celery was left out because its stalk is a petiole.

misconceptions.evidence: Built around documented plant misconceptions in primary science research: plants get food from the soil, a tree is not a plant, flowers are only decorative, water enters through the leaves, and a carrot is a fruit. Each one is a locked prediction choice (roots at the top, water falls on the leaves, a tree is too big, a carrot is a fruit) or a tagged challenge slip with a correcting line.

lab_distinct.evidence: New flagplant lab, not reused from the seed or sprout labs: a two-tap label-and-place plant builder, a part-to-job matching board, a dye-water animation where blue drops climb roots then stem then leaves and a white flower turns blue, a tree labelling scene with trunk and branches, and a food sorter into root, stem, leaf and flower bins. It passed the 30% shingle gate against every other flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The sequence goes from naming and placing the four parts, to what each part does, to seeing water travel through them in order, to transferring the same plan onto a tree, and finally to recognising the parts in everyday foods. The child acts before each reveal, and every success line restates the idea, for example 'Water goes in at the roots and up'.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options: where roots grow (at the top or on the leaves), how water reaches the leaves (falls on them like rain), whether a tree is a plant (too big, made of wood), and which part a carrot is (a fruit or a leaf). The next step makes the child produce the right answer, and the reveal line says whether the guess held up.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with eleven tagged slips, covering soil as food, trees not being plants, carrot as fruit or stem, flowers as only pretty, leaves taking in water, and mixing up trunk with roots or branches. Each message names the slip in plain words and gives the right fact, e.g. 'A woody stem is still a stem, so a tree is a plant'.

readability.evidence: The kid text is written for ages 5 to 6 with short sentences of mostly one-syllable words about roots, stems, a straw and bees, well under the family kid target. The adult text uses the exact curriculum terms (deciduous, evergreen, basic structure, absorb, photosynthesis named for Year 3) with plain glosses. Canvas lines stay short and every prompt names the part to tap.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler scan and the 12% similarity gate against the neighbouring lessons 426 (growing from a seed) and 331 (plants need water and light). This lesson keeps to structure and jobs rather than germination or growth conditions. Each kid paragraph adds one part or the tree, and the adult paragraphs cover the standards, the jobs, the named mistakes and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: I checked screenshots at 360 px Android in light theme and iPhone 13 in dark theme for every step, both before and during Show me. The leaves and stem labels overlapped at first, so I moved the stem slot below the leaves and checked again. The label cards and the food grid fit without clipping, the six food bins stay readable, and the young class gives 56 px tap buttons.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations and no console errors. Every tap or drag on the canvas has a labelled button twin (part labels, places, jobs, Water the soil, food and bin buttons), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each spoken line, so the water order can also be followed by ear.
